hook: A medical encyclopedia that gives you whatever you read about sounds like a doomsday object, and the article starts by treating it that way. Pay attention to the object class line and the very first revision, because they hint at where things are going. It reads like a lab report that slowly loses its composure, and the test log includes D-class subjects being killed and vivisected.
whyItMatters: It is a sharp example of an article whose real subject is the Foundation's own paranoia rather than the anomaly. Instead of escalating the threat, it escalates the staff's reactions, and the payoff comes from an administrator looking back at the whole effort. The panicked name-dropping of other disease anomalies makes it a small satire of how researchers, and readers, jump to the worst case.
thingsToNotice:
Watch the notes change across the test log. Subjects who read about lung cancer are executed, autopsied, and in one case cut open alive until he dies of shock, yet no tumor is ever found; the corrections struck through mid-sentence show the writers' certainty slipping. By the time a researcher who never read the book starts coughing and looks slightly taller, the note-taker is convinced he has turned into an escaped plague carrier.

The recovery team finds the isolated site wrecked by fear alone: two researchers in biohazard suits who used up nearly all the air tanks, an agent creeping through the ducts with a gun drawn, the suspected carrier barricaded with a homemade flamethrower, and another agent dead inside a closet he had taped airtight. The O5 memo then states that no unusual pathogen was found anywhere, labels the whole thing hypochondria by proxy, and orders the book locked away, which is exactly what the downgraded class at the top was telling you.
